items.question: What makes you suspect that next-token prediction has an inherent flaw?
items.object: Next-token prediction
items.answer: Everyone knows that images are created by nature. No matter how humans understand them, they are simply there. But something happened at the time that left us utterly baffled. Then we found some clues. For example, larger models tend to skip steps when solving math problems. This may point directly to an inherent flaw in what we do—next-token prediction.

items.question: How do you understand the role of scaling in the success of XNet and your subsequent work on ResNet?
items.object: Scaling as the driving force behind deep learning
items.answer:
I think the greatest driving force behind deep learning has been scaling. XNet’s method was actually no different from the earlier deep-learning framework, but its biggest difference was that it did scaling. It happened to reach the best historical moment of that time. In today’s terms, scaling requires simultaneously scaling the model, data, and compute. ImageNet had provided more than 1.2 million images; at the time, simply running through it was already not easy. CUDA performance had become very good around 2012, so there was compute support as well. At that point, the most important question was who could scale up the model. Earlier neural networks were only a few megabytes; XNet made one over 700 megabytes. That opportunity is why it succeeded.

I was doing my PhD at exactly that time and continued along the same route. From 2012 to 2016, what I was doing was model scaling: I wanted to make models bigger. That means greater width, greater depth, and, for visual signals, greater resolution. We worked on resolution, and we proposed MSRA init to address width scaling. Depth was the hardest part. Earlier models would see performance fall rapidly beyond a dozen or so layers. ResNet could take a network from a dozen layers to dozens, hundreds, or even thousands.

After that series of work, I felt model scaling was basically solved, at least at that time. Continuing to make models bigger no longer produced particularly large gains; the baton had shifted back to data and compute. That was why, after graduating, I went to Megvii to work on small models.
quotes: Everyone knows that XNet—its method was actually no different from the earlier deep-learning framework, but its biggest difference was that it did scaling. So you can see that the greatest driving force behind deep learning—AI deep learning—has been scaling. And XNet was very successful; everyone knows that. Why? Because it happened to reach the best historical moment of that time. In today’s terms, scaling requires simultaneously scaling the model, data, and compute.

Around 2012, as someone from computer vision, I knew that in 2009 Li Feifei’s team had proposed ImageNet, a dataset of more than 1.2 million images. At the time, simply running through it was already not easy. So data scaling could be considered no longer a problem at that point: someone had provided a very large dataset. As for compute, everyone knows NVIDIA introduced CUDA in 2009. It was initially for scientific computing, but around 2012 CUDA performance had become very good, so there was some compute support as well. Thus, compute scaling could also be considered solved. At that point, the most important question was who would be first—or who could—scale up the model. XNet succeeded at that. The neural networks we had been making before were only a few megabytes; all at once, it made one over 700 megabytes. That opportunity is why XNet succeeded.

I was doing my PhD at exactly that time and continued along the same route. Throughout my PhD, from 2012 to 2016, what I was doing was model scaling: I wanted to make models bigger and keep doing that. Making models bigger means greater width, greater depth, and, for visual signals, greater resolution. Kaiming and Sinian gave me a great deal of guidance on this, and we proposed multiple methods together. For example, we scaled up resolution. For width scaling, one encounters exploding or vanishing gradients, so we proposed an initialization strategy called MSRA init, which addressed width scaling quite well. Depth was the hardest part. Earlier models would see performance fall rapidly once they went beyond a dozen or so layers. At that time, we proposed ResNet, which has had greater impact. It could take a network from a dozen layers to dozens, hundreds, or even thousands of layers. After completing that series of work, I felt that model scaling was basically solved, at least at that time. After graduating, I went to Megvii to work on small models. The reason was that continuing to make models bigger no longer produced particularly large gains; the baton had shifted back to data and compute.

items.question: How do you judge the importance of architecture design when moving from large models to small models deployed on specific hardware?
items.object: Architecture design for large models versus hardware-constrained small models
items.answer:
I found that making a model small from a large model involves a very, very different way of thinking. People may imagine that model architecture and design details are crucial, but people who have done architecture work probably know that architecture often does not matter. Especially for large models, architecture design is more about getting the broad direction right. If you use ResNet, for example, the precise way its layers are connected does not matter much. Performance differences are not large.

But once you shrink the compute quota, say for deployment on-device, the details become very important. Runtime behavior and efficiency differ greatly across hardware devices. When I was working on ShafaNet, I felt deeply how difficult this was: to make a model for a specific task run on specific hardware, with the highest efficiency and performance, requires a great deal of experience-driven design.

So after several projects on small models, my research shifted mainly toward how to design these complex small models generally or automatically. In 2017 and 2018, I started working on neural architecture search, NAS, using automation to design models that could run efficiently on specific hardware. The 2019 work called SPOS could, at very low cost, search for the best-performing model on a target dataset for a given piece of hardware. That greatly freed people from manual work.

Architecture design, especially for large models, is more about getting the broad direction right. As long as the broad direction is right—if you use ResNet, for example—the precise way its layers are connected does not matter much. Performance differences are not large. The key is the broad direction. But once you shrink the compute quota, say for deployment on-device, the details of the architecture design become very important. Its runtime behavior and efficiency differ greatly across hardware devices.

items.question: What do you see as the main reason BERT and GPT opened up a scalable research path for natural language processing?
items.object: The source of NLP's progress with BERT and GPT
items.answer:
When I turned back toward large models at the end of 2019, the difficulty was very different from before 2016. Earlier, the main storyline was how to make models bigger. By 2016, the main difficulty had become data scaling. Computer vision had developed for many years, but it still lacked something like the GPT moment or BERT moment in NLP.

In 2019, NLP was making enormous progress. Many people said this was because of Transformers, but I do not think it was. Architecture is not the primary factor here; the primary factor is the optimization method. NLP used to be the same as CV: when I got a batch of data, I had to label a large batch of labels. As long as you rely on manual annotation, you can never scale up.

NLP was fortunate enough to discover certain training methods. BERT used something like a cloze task. It may appear unrelated to the countless downstream tasks we need to do, but first, this upstream task does not need labels and can scale indefinitely. Second, the more data there is, the stronger representations the network can learn through that task, and the better it does downstream. GPT’s decoder-only, next-token-prediction approach went further: it does not require labels, and somehow it can also unify many downstream tasks through in-context modeling. Of course, many of these insights came only after GPT-3 appeared in 2020. But at least the NLP route had been fully opened up.

Before 2016, the main storyline was how to make models bigger: model scaling. By 2016, however, the main difficulty was data scaling. Computer vision had developed for many years. Although self-supervised and label-free methods kept appearing, it had always lacked something like the GPT moment or BERT moment in NLP.

In 2019, NLP was making enormous progress. Many people said this was because of Transformers, but it was not. As I said earlier, architecture is not the primary factor here; the primary factor is the optimization method. NLP was fortunate enough to discover certain training methods. BERT, for example, used something like a cloze task. It may appear unrelated to the countless downstream tasks we need to do, but through this upstream task, first, it does not need labels and can scale indefinitely. Second, it found that the more data there is, the stronger representations a neural network can learn through the upstream task, and the better it does on downstream tasks. GPT’s decoder-only, next-token-prediction approach went further: not only does it not require labels, but somehow it can also unify many downstream tasks through in-context modeling. Of course, many of these insights came only after GPT-3 appeared in 2020. At least the NLP route had been fully opened up.

items.question: Why did you become skeptical that contrastive learning and masked image modeling could deliver computer vision's equivalent of a BERT or GPT moment?
items.object: The scaling limits of contrastive learning and masked image modeling
items.answer:
With MoCo and SimCLR, people saw hope again. Fully self-supervised feature learning was beginning to approach the results trained on fully labeled ImageNet data, although there was still a gap. That was very encouraging. But the industry, including us, put a great deal of effort into studying these methods and found that many worked only on small models. Once scaled up very large, their performance rapidly deteriorated.

Then ViT made the pure-Transformer architecture work in CV, and people naturally brought NLP methods over. Especially after Kaiming proposed MAE, self-supervised performance on downstream tasks after fine-tuning was no worse than, and sometimes slightly better than, corresponding fully supervised models. The community was excited again. But I remained cautiously optimistic, because I had done many things on small models, and many of these results were on small models. On large models, they did not have NLP-like scale-up properties.

By the end of 2021, I had roughly figured out why. Both contrastive learning and MIM learn a kind of invariance. Invariance is extremely important for visual representation, but the invariance these methods learn is not data-driven; it is handcrafted. Contrastive learning depends heavily on augmentation. Its negative-sample part can be regarded as a regularizer that encourages maximum entropy and prevents information collapse. But its numerator learns an invariance supplied by the manually designed augmentation. That takes us back to manual design.

NLP truly learned from data: with a higher-quality corpus, the model could learn more associations, model its distribution, and learn more knowledge through compression. In CV, whether you design rotation, color augmentation, or multi-crop invariance, the features satisfy only the invariances you designed. A small amount of data is enough to teach that, and there is no additional information.

I saw MIM’s ceiling early: it learned occlusion invariance. If I cover a bottle of water and reveal only its top, a human can still guess that there is a bottle behind it. That is important, but it is only a necessary condition, not a sufficient one. With little data, learning occlusion-invariant features is very useful. But even if you expand the data, you are still learning that one invariance; you are not eliciting more invariances from the data. That is the key problem. In early 2022, I published an opinion piece arguing that MIM did not have a large scaling law or obvious scaling. Quite a few people criticized me, but now it seems few people are pursuing that route, and it is indeed not so effective.
quotes: Then by the end of 2019, work such as MoCo and SimCLR appeared, and people saw hope again. Could contrastive learning be the CV equivalent of the BERT or GPT moment in NLP? In particular, people saw that, across many metrics, fully self-supervised feature learning was beginning to approach—though still with some gap at the time—the results trained on fully labeled ImageNet data. That was very encouraging. But the whole industry, including us, invested a great deal of effort in studying it and found that many of these methods worked only on small models. They still did not have scale-up properties. Once scaled up very large, their performance rapidly deteriorated.

Then in 2020 there was another major event in CV: someone made the pure-Transformer architecture work thoroughly in CV. That was the ViT series, which is still used today. People doing research naturally thought: great, we can bring all the NLP methods over to CV and try them.

Especially after Kaiming proposed the MAE series, we could see that in self-supervision their performance—particularly on downstream tasks after fine-tuning—was no worse than, and sometimes slightly exceeded, models trained with corresponding fully supervised signals. This made the CV community excited again. But I remained cautiously optimistic, because I had done many things on small models and many of these methods were on small models. Once you put them on large models, you find that they do not have NLP-like scale-up properties at all.

By roughly the end of 2021, I carefully analyzed why early contrastive-learning work did not work on large models. MIM might work somewhat better, but I still did not favor it. I had roughly figured out why. The reason is that both contrastive learning and MIM somehow learn a kind of invariance. Invariance is indeed extremely important for CV representation, especially visual representation. But the invariance learned by these two methods is not data-driven; it is entirely handcrafted. Contrastive learning depends very heavily on augmentation—on the way you construct it. Its negative-sample part can be regarded as a regularizer that encourages maximum entropy and prevents information collapse. But its numerator learns a kind of invariance, and that invariance is not given by the data; it is given by the manually designed augmentation. This takes us back to the old path of manual design. Why did NLP work so well? It truly learned from data. The higher-quality corpus I have, the more associations in that corpus the model can learn, model its distribution, and learn more knowledge through compression. CV cannot do this. Whatever invariance you design—rotation, color augmentation, or multi-crop invariance—the features it ultimately learns satisfy only those invariances you designed. Naturally, there is no scale-up effect, because a small amount of data is enough to teach the model that, and there is no additional information.

At the time, many people rushed into MIM, which was essentially a BERT-like method. But I saw its ceiling early: it learned occlusion invariance. Occlusion invariance is indeed important. For example, when humans recognize a bottle of water, if I cover up the bottle and reveal only its top, humans can still guess that it is a bottle of water behind it. Seeing a local part is enough. That is occlusion invariance in human cognition. But having occlusion-invariant features is only a necessary condition, not a sufficient one. With MIM, when the data volume is small, the algorithm’s design can enable you to learn features with occlusion invariance. That is very good and useful. But even if you expand the data volume, you are still learning only this one invariance. It does not elicit more invariances from the data. That is the key reason it does not work. So in early 2022, I published an opinion piece arguing that MIM was not useful: it did not have a large scaling law or obvious scaling. I was criticized by quite a few people in the field, but now it seems that few people are pursuing this route, and it is indeed not so effective.

items.question: How did your understanding of the limits of static-image learning shape the path you chose toward visual intelligence?
items.object: Static-image learning and the path toward visual intelligence
items.answer:
Starting in 2022, I became relatively pessimistic that intelligence could be learned purely from the visual domain, especially static images. People had spent so many years developing self-supervised methods, yet none seemed to acquire properties as readily as NLP did. Then I read Jason Wei’s papers on chain of thought and emergent abilities, and I was greatly shaken. After all those years, I was still studying representation, while colleagues in NLP were already studying reasoning and higher-level intelligent properties.

I began comparing natural language and static images from three perspectives: generation, understanding, and alignment with humans. Video is an exception; it may contain richer information. But under the GPT framework, those three things are three-in-one for natural language. If I model its joint probability, I simultaneously have generation, understanding, and human alignment. The preceding text affects the distribution of following text, and the model can produce words that match it. That is a kind of understanding. I can constrain it with prompts and ask arbitrary questions about the preceding text; sampling the conditional probability of subsequent text can produce answers. And the training corpus comes from humans. By modeling natural human language, it naturally achieves alignment with humans.

For images, those things are not a closed loop. I can build a generative model that captures an image dataset’s joint probability distribution and consider myself to have obtained all the information in the data. But can it understand? Clearly not. There are countless ways to model the joint distribution among pixels, with no constraint requiring the modeling to conform to human understanding. Images objectively exist; they come from nature. How humans understand them is generally not information contained in the image. Images containing text may be an exception.

MIM and contrastive learning work to some extent because they inject human understanding. For me, understanding a cup requires occlusion invariance: I still know it is a cup if part is covered. But an animal, an alien creature, or a robot does not have to understand the image in the human way. That invariance is not contained in the image. Understanding and generation split apart. Video might compensate through different viewing angles, but I can only say it is possible; using video effectively is much harder, and its information density is much lower. Human alignment is also absent from images coming from nature. So I believe it is difficult to obtain the kind of intelligence humans mean by doing more on static images alone.

In 2022, I basically stopped researching static-image representation learning. Vision is certainly indispensable to a genuine AGI system, but I did not think we could get there just through contrastive learning or MLM. My short-term direction was to use alignment between vision and language. The internet has massive amounts of interleaved image-text material: web pages, papers, journals, magazines, and public-account posts. If we embed images in a text stream, perhaps we can use text’s union of understanding, generation, and human alignment to give the system intelligent capabilities through that alignment.

In the long term, those materials have significant bias and limitations. They rarely include detailed visual processes, especially physical motion. More of that data is in video. So I thought we still needed to explore visual intelligence through video, and even embodied systems. After 2022, I had a relatively short-term goal and a relatively long-term goal, and the framework for building visual multimodal large models had become very clear to me.
quotes: So starting in 2022, I became relatively pessimistic that intelligence could be learned by relying purely on the visual domain, especially static images—that there could be a GPT moment in CV. For one thing, people had researched it for so many years and developed all kinds of self-supervised methods, yet none seemed to acquire properties as readily as NLP did. In particular, in 2022, after I read two papers—both by Jason Wei—one about the discovery of chain of thought, and the other about emergent abilities, I was greatly shaken. I felt that after all these years of research, I was still at the level of representation, while colleagues in NLP had already begun studying reasoning and higher-level intelligent properties.

Let us compare natural-language data with static images from three perspectives—generation, understanding, and alignment with humans. Video is an exception; it may contain richer information. But at least for natural language, under the GPT framework, generation, understanding, and alignment with humans are three-in-one. If I make a generative model like GPT and model its joint probability, then I simultaneously have generation, understanding, and human alignment. Why? In a GPT-like closed loop, when the preceding text is given and the model outputs the conditional probability of following text, the preceding text necessarily affects the distribution of following text. The model can output words that match the preceding text. That is a kind of understanding. You can ask it to output something in the middle and constrain it with prompts; you can ask arbitrary questions about the preceding text. In modeling the joint probability, it samples the conditional probability of subsequent text and can answer questions about the preceding text. We can regard that as generation; naturally it is, because GPT itself is a generative model. And the corpus used for pretraining and training comes from humans—natural human language. By modeling that distribution, it naturally achieves alignment with humans.

Now look back at an image from those same three dimensions: generation, understanding, and human alignment. You find that images—especially static images—are not a closed loop. Why? Given an image or an image dataset, what is the model that can obtain the most information and make the fullest use of that dataset? It must be a generative model. I can make a generative model that captures the joint probability distribution of the image dataset. Once I have made that model, I consider myself to have obtained all the information in the data. But can it understand? Clearly not. The dataset models all its images and the joint distribution among every pixel. I can model that joint distribution in countless ways, but there is no constraint requiring the modeling approach to happen to conform to the human way of understanding the image. Images objectively exist; they come from nature. Information about how humans understand them is not contained in the image. A small number of images, such as images containing text, may contain human understanding of them. But in general, images are created by nature. No matter how humans understand them, they are simply there. Therefore, an image does not necessarily include human understanding of it; it lacks this kind of information.

Why can MIM or contrastive learning somehow work to a certain extent? Put plainly, it still injects human understanding. If I do not inject into this image the notion that its features need to have some kind of invariance, the image itself cannot possess such invariance. For humans, understanding a cup requires occlusion invariance: even if I cover part of it, I still know it is a cup. But does an animal, an alien creature, or a robot have to understand this image in the human way? Of course not. In other words, this invariance is not contained in the image. So you find that understanding and generation split apart, at least in the dimension of static images. Many people ask whether video can compensate for this, because video may be filmed from different angles and naturally have this kind of occlusion invariance. I can only say it is possible. But effective use of video data is much harder than using static images, and its information density is much lower. Finally, human alignment is even more clearly absent. The corpus for language models is generated by humans; if you train a generative model on it, its distribution naturally aligns with the distribution produced by humans. Images come from nature, so they may not be aligned—or rather, they definitely are not aligned. For static images, understanding, generation, and alignment with humans are split apart. In other words, no matter how much you do on static images, I believe it is difficult to form the kind of intelligence humans mean by intelligence.

Having reached this point of view, in 2022 I basically stopped research on representation learning for static images. For a genuine AGI system or intelligent system, vision is certainly an indispensable module, but we cannot truly get there in the visual domain merely by doing contrastive learning or MLM the way we do now. I then roughly conceived a direction. In the short term, we could make use of the alignment between vision and language. On the internet there are massive amounts of interleaved image-text data—web pages, papers, journals and magazines, public-account posts—that are often organized in interleaved, mixed image-text form. The image world itself has difficulty expressing many things. But if images are embedded in the stream of text, could we use text’s closed-loop nature—the union of understanding, generation, and human alignment that I just described—to enable an intelligent system to have intelligent capabilities through this alignment? That was the most readily conceived short-term approach. In the long term, such materials have very significant bias and major limitations. For example, they rarely include very detailed visual processes, especially physical motion. More of that data is in video. In the long term, we still need to explore the possibility of visual intelligence through video, and even embodied systems. After 2022, though, the framework and the idea of building visual multimodal large models around the model had already become very clear to me. I had a relatively short-term goal and a relatively long-term goal, so I went for it.

items.question: Why do you think the large-model efforts of 2021 produced disappointing results?
items.object: The disappointing results of the 2021 large-model wave
items.answer:
The timing at the end of 2022 was awkward. In 2021, especially in China, there had been a wave of enthusiasm for large models. After GPT-3 came out, people announced models with tens of billions, hundreds of billions, or even trillions of parameters, but ultimately they did not achieve very good results. Most people did not believe the story anymore.

I think there were mainly two reasons. The first is the old refrain: data quality. Base models, especially before instruction tuning, were truly difficult to use, could do few things, and performed poorly. More importantly, I think people severely underestimated the role of data in scaling laws. When GPT-3 first appeared, it used hundreds of billions of parameters but only several hundred billion data tokens. By today’s view, that was essentially completely inverted. With a model that large, if you do not give it tens of trillions or even dozens of trillions of data tokens, you are doing it an injustice. Models at the time were severely undertrained.

Those two reasons meant that people trying to reproduce GPT-3 in 2021 could not get particularly good results. But very quickly, at the end of 2022, ChatGPT appeared and immediately proved many people wrong. It turned out this could be made very useful, and it felt extremely promising—as though the age of intelligence was about to arrive.

items.question: How did your first attempt at interleaved image-text pretraining change your understanding of what it takes to unify multimodal generation and understanding?
items.object: Unifying multimodal generation and understanding through interleaved image-text pretraining
items.answer:
Looking back now, I greatly underestimated the difficulty. My idea at the time was very simple. Whether on the internet or in books, there is massive interleaved image-text data. Since we had verified that language next-word prediction works, I would simply find a way to use a tokenizer to align images to the same space as language. When I encountered text, I would predict text; when I encountered an image, I would predict an image. So in 2023, when we built our first-generation language model, Step-1, we followed exactly that route. We did not first build a purely language model. We included multimodal data from the very beginning of pretraining. Because directly generating images autoregressively was still somewhat worse at that time, I attached a pretrained diffusion module for image generation.

Its text performance was about the same as training directly on text, and its image-understanding performance was especially good. We found that images and text aligned extremely well. For example, if you wrote words on an image and asked questions about them, the result was almost the same as performing OCR on those words and then asking questions. The model could already freely use information from text and images together in thinking; it seemed to have no obstacle.

But generation was especially poor. The understanding component—the language component—had very, very poor control over the visual component. More interestingly, at a certain stage of training, I removed the generation component and found that it had absolutely no impact on the understanding component’s performance. Put plainly, the generation component may have been useless. This was a major blow to us. Architecturally, the system seemed to achieve unified generation and understanding: it could generate and understand images, and generate and understand text. items.question: What did your attempt to iteratively align separate visual generation and understanding models teach you about their relationship?
items.object: Iteratively aligning separate visual generation and understanding models
items.answer:
Throughout 2024, our generation and understanding were iterated separately. I also observed that major overseas companies did the same. For understanding, OpenAI had been bringing language, audio—especially after 4o—visual understanding, and later video understanding into one model; Gemini did similarly. But generation had always been done separately, following the DALL-E-to-Sora route. We also followed this route, while continually looking for an opportunity to merge them.

A generative model needs to construct pairs of text and visual signals. I could use my latest understanding model to label data, thereby building a better visual-generation model; then attach that generation model to the understanding model and continue training the understanding model, so that the generation model could provide gradients to guide the understanding model. After one such iteration, I thought the gap between generation and understanding could shrink. Then I could use the understanding model to label data for the generation model again, train the next-generation model, and in turn use that for understanding again. I wondered whether the gap would become smaller and smaller, until I could train them together. I would have an initial system whose two sides were sufficiently aligned; put them together and run the whole loop.

But after more than half a year, it still did not work. I got an increasingly powerful understanding model and an increasingly powerful generation model, but putting them together did not produce one plus one greater than two. You can always put them together, but they still behaved like two models. If I removed either one, the other was unaffected: it became neither stronger nor weaker. There was no combined effect at all.

Understanding’s effect on generation was even worse. Although I labeled so much data and jointly trained for so long, the controllability of my generation branch was still very poor. It often generated distorted fonts, violations of geometric constraints, and—especially in video generation—large numbers of video signals violating physical constraints. If I directly fed such a signal to the understanding model, it could accurately tell me that it violated common sense. It knew that itself, but it could not control itself from generating images that conspicuously violated physical common sense or spatial-perspective relations. This issue remained stuck there. I had not figured out how to solve it. After working for more than half a year on unified generation and understanding, I was very lost.

items.question: How did training your trillion-parameter Savi2 model change your view of the relationship between model scale and capability?
items.object: Scaling language models and the nonmonotonic behavior of mathematical reasoning
items.answer:
By the end of 2023, we had finished Savi1, a multimodal model trained on mixed, interleaved data with roughly over 100 billion parameters. Naturally, I thought the amount of data was now sufficient and perhaps the compute was sufficient too, so at the beginning of 2024 we launched a larger model, Savi2. It had a trillion parameters, and its activation was very large—over 200 billion active parameters. It was a true giant.

Once training began, we found that the investment was simply a bottomless pit. We had greatly underestimated how much data was required to train such a large model. If data is insufficient, simply scaling the model up enormously produces poor results. It needs a huge amount of data. As data grows, compute demand grows proportionally as well. If you scale both parameter count and data volume, compute demand becomes quadratic. We trained this model with enormous difficulty. The project took more than nine months, but we finally trained it to a state we considered fairly satisfactory.

But something happened that left us utterly baffled. We generally believe that as data and models grow, model capabilities should grow across the board. Yet Savi2 was extremely strong in humanities subjects, including writing, but in science subjects—especially mathematics—it performed worse than a 7B model. And it was very difficult to improve its math or logical ability through alignment. This was extraordinary, because at the time the whole community believed that the bigger the model, the better it should be in general.

At first we thought our data quality was poor, or it had not trained long enough. But after a series of very rigorous tests, we trained a series of small models—from 1B to 7B, then 30B and 70B. We found that a model’s general conversational ability, particularly its emotional intelligence, and its breadth of knowledge really did become stronger as it grew. But its reasoning ability—especially relatively constrained, local reasoning ability such as mathematics—first rose, then leveled off, and then declined as it was scaled further.

items.question: Why do you think next-token prediction can make larger language models less reliable at mathematical reasoning?
items.object: Next-token prediction and the deterioration of mathematical reasoning as models scale
items.answer:
We found some clues: on math problems, larger models are more inclined to skip steps. Smaller models may be much weaker, but when handling a long chain of arithmetic, no matter how simple, they honestly calculate step by step. A larger model, when adding three numbers, often gives up the step-by-step derivation and blurts out the final result. Most skipped steps are right, but a small fraction are wrong. And in math, one wrong step makes the final answer completely wrong. That caught my attention.

Much of our training corpus comes from the internet, though it also includes lots of verified data. I can guarantee that verified data rarely skips steps. But internet data often omits intermediate reasoning. That makes it easy to understand why large models skip steps. But why do relatively small models instead not skip them? After analysis, I believe this is a fundamental flaw of next-token prediction.

Fundamentally, it models a joint probability distribution: during optimization, the model adjusts its outputs to make their distribution increasingly close to the input-data distribution. Another way to understand it is compression. The more accurately a compressor estimates the joint probability, the lower the bitrate it can achieve in lossless compression. But for math problems there is a fundamental gap: a higher compression ratio does not necessarily mean higher computational accuracy.

Consider a thought experiment. Suppose a dataset contains many operations adding a dozen or so numbers. Maybe 50% comes from ordinary internet text, which simply gives the final result after an equals sign. The other data includes the process, honestly adding the numbers one by one. At the maximum-compression optimum, the model should have a 50% probability of directly outputting the answer and a 50% probability of outputting it step by step. That is theoretically optimal. But for a small model, directly blurting out the answer is too complex for its limited parameters to fit. So it can learn only the step-by-step mode.

This is the classic phenomenon called feature exploration in generative models. A diffusion model models simpler images first; only with more model capacity or training time does it gradually characterize the full distribution. Large models are different. We tried something like Stan Pool, with more than 20 billion activations. It really can add a dozen two-digit numbers and directly state the final answer, correctly with high probability—perhaps over 90%. Of course, it may also calculate step by step.

If compression is the standard, the large model is better: it is closer to the original distribution. The small model has simply lost one mode. But for a math problem, the primary requirement is getting the answer right, not making the output distribution closer to the pretraining corpus. Whether small or large, if a model calculates step by step, these simple numerical operations are almost never wrong. But large models tend to think they can do it: they take the shortcut. They may be correct 90% of the time, but the remaining 10% is fatal. As the logic becomes more complex and there are more steps, those small error probabilities accumulate, and the overall error rate rises sharply—often becoming far worse than what smaller models can achieve. This is a very bad phenomenon, and it may point directly to a fundamental flaw in next-token prediction.

items.question: How do you understand the role of rule-based reinforcement learning in heavily pretrained language models?
items.object: Rule-based reinforcement learning in heavily pretrained language models
items.answer:
If maximizing compression and the task itself have a gap, it is better to directly optimize the task we care about. That is the rationale behind RL. Rule-based RL seems to have exactly the right objective: it leaves distribution fitting behind and goes straight for the goal—regardless of what happens in the middle, just get the goal right. Larger models like to skip steps, but any skipped step lowers their chance of reaching the correct answer. Thus rule-based RL substantially mitigates their tendency to skip steps. It lets them find the most reliable path. It helps especially more for large models because their baseline is lower; small models benefit too, and it stabilizes their reasoning chains. But overall the gains were still small. Many problems they could not solve before, they still could not solve.

I think the key reason language-model RL differs from conventional game-playing and control is language pretraining, and it is very heavy pretraining. Game-playing and control often start from scratch or have only light pretraining. In conventional RL, reward signals can be excessively sparse and hard to estimate. You need techniques that encourage exploration; you might need MCTS to search branches far into the future and slowly propagate rewards backward. But in O1 work, people found that adding MCTS seemed to be of no use. A PRM is not completely useless, but at least for the problems studied so far—perhaps they are too simple, perhaps for other reasons—conventional RL methodologies work very differently for language models.

Solving a math problem can require thousands or tens of thousands of tokens, with the entire vocabulary as the action space at each step. Under those conditions, all current RL algorithms would be helpless. But after pretraining, the model has seen many types of math problems of differing difficulty—perhaps every kind in the world. This enormously compresses its feature space, and therefore its action space.

I have done some statistics: in an output sequence of four or five thousand tokens, there may be fewer than ten critical decisions that affect the final result. Once it enters a branch, all those many tokens are basically automatic. Those tokens are not really in the search space that RL must solve. The actual problem for RL is the small number of critical branches—critical tokens.

This also explains why, even before RL training, there can be a nontrivial probability of randomly rolling out a correct answer. In many traditional RL settings, you cannot just wander around and suddenly beat the game. But for not-too-hard language-model questions, perhaps over half are already solved correctly at the start. Even for hard questions, if I roll out 100 times, several may be entirely correct with no process supervision, just random sampling.

So RL should make the model focus on the key tokens and get them right. The model may roll out correctly many times, but not reliably: one rollout is right, another wrong. Choose the correct branch, and you solve it; the probabilities already compressed away by pretraining need not be considered.

items.question: What do you see as the essential breakthrough behind O1's success?
items.object: O1's reflection patterns and the idea of meta-CoT
items.answer:
I think it is entirely fair to regard the O1 moment as a kind of benchmark moment. Many people think the difference is RL algorithms or data evolution, but it is not. The algorithm is still the same rule-based kind. The central reason is the pattern of the chain of thought. People in this field often say that making O1, or a thinking model, is essentially “pattern is all you need.” Find the best organizational pattern for the chain of thought, then use RL to bring it out. Which RL algorithm you choose is not crucial. PPO, JPO, or even primitive policy-gradient-based methods—there is no essential difference.

At some step the model faces two branches. Can choosing left versus right be resolved within one token? For many problems, I believe it cannot. The simplest example is multiplication. Asking today's language models to do large-number multiplication in one shot is almost impossible to get right. The core reason is complexity. Large-number multiplication is at least O(N²); if you want to argue, it is O(N log N), but in any case it is greater than O(N). A transformer's single-step computation is O(N). If a task exceeds that complexity, it is unlikely to be resolved within one token.

The search space may be small—perhaps only ten critical tokens—but for a sufficiently complex math problem, you cannot immediately decide which construction or algorithm is needed at an intermediate point. Many math problems depend on clever constructions. Inequalities in particular often depend on them. At the instant you choose a construction, you can only go by intuition; until you calculate through it, you do not know whether it works. If humans cannot make this advance judgment because it is too complex, why should a Transformer be able to?

That is why, before the O1 paradigm, even with rule-based RL, we could observe reward increasing but then hitting a ceiling. A problem may be correct six times out of ten, yet wrong four times out of ten forever. At its critical decisions it lacks sufficient evidence to choose the correct path within one token. Perhaps a very similar problem has a few different numbers, and the branch selected 40% of the time is the correct one there. With both kinds of data present, always selecting the 60% branch would fail the other class and would not maximize accuracy.

At this point the solution is obvious: allow it to follow both branches. That is exactly the motivation for introducing reflection. This is O-series' greatest achievement: it truly adds reflection to the computation process.

RL can produce reflection by itself. Experiments show that if you run long enough, it can generate reflection without manually injecting it, but with very low probability, great time cost, and poor results. Again, this is because of pretraining. Pretraining is crucial because it prunes and greatly compresses the action space. But for reflection it over-compresses that space. Human corpora contain very little reflection data. People typically provide correct solution processes, not the erroneous paths and detours they took. After sufficient compression, the model believes every problem should smoothly go directly from the first CoT step to the end. Reflection tokens exist, but their probability is extremely low.

The O-style approach can use pattern injection to inject those reflection patterns back in, effectively expanding the action space. If at a critical token it does not know whether to go left or right, it can choose one, continue to the end, realize it is wrong, go back, and proceed from the earlier point.

So I think O1 is, in a sense, a meta-CoT. CoT improves accuracy by dividing a problem into steps, ensuring each step stays within the model's complexity limit. But for more complex problems, you cannot see at a glance which CoT path to take. By introducing reflection patterns, O1 is essentially a CoT for choosing CoTs. items.question: Why do you think current image-generation methods are still in the era of one-shot answers?
items.object: The lack of chain-of-thought reasoning in autoregressive and diffusion image generation
items.answer:
The defining characteristic of autoregression is that moves cannot be undone. Once you draw a region, you cannot change it. That means a neural network must decide, in a single inference step, how to draw that portion. It is unclear whether that task exceeds the Transformer's single-step complexity limit, but we can construct thought experiments where it absolutely does. For example, ask it to draw a blackboard and write a complete solution and answer to a chicken-and-rabbit problem on it. It looks like an image-generation task, but concealed beneath it is a math problem with many steps. Many of those steps clearly exceed a Transformer's one-step reasoning capability. Regardless of how well it draws, merely solving the problem correctly cannot be done by current tokens, or in one shot.

Diffusion may be somewhat better because it is multi-step. If it is flow matching, it is an ODE, so it is a multi-step process. But I definitely do not believe that process contains reasoning. Denoising constructs a stochastic process that makes it easier for the system to fit an unknown distribution using a known one. It is clearly unlike how humans generate images. A human artist usually sketches first, then draws outlines, then key internal elements, colors, and finally renders. They do not use an eraser to remove noise bit by bit and recover every local region that way. Humans draw while strictly following their semantic understanding of the scene; the process is strongly semantic. They move from one object to another, from outlines to details. In denoising it is hard to say which step is semantic or object-level; to it, everything is merely noise to generate.

So I do not think it differs much from autoregression. You can regard the entire diffusion process as one generation step: semantics may be completely determined at some diffusion step, and the rest only fills in details. Whether you use autoregression or diffusion, in my view you remain in the language model's most primitive one-shot form. You give it a problem and demand that it generate the image directly in one step. Of course the result will be poor, because its complexity simply cannot meet the requirements needed to complete the task. So on the generation side, I think the biggest problem is the lack of CoT—something analogous to CoT in language models. In fact, it is already two generations behind language models. It lacks not only meta-CoT; it does not even have CoT. It is still in that earlier era of one-shot answers.

items.question: Why do you see chain of thought in visual understanding as the starting point for bringing visual generation and understanding together?
items.object: Visual-space chain of thought as a bridge between visual understanding and generation
items.answer: Around the end of last year, I concluded that simply putting generation and understanding together would be extremely difficult; a very large link was missing between them. That link is CoT. It is relatively difficult to do CoT directly in generation. Drawing on language models, it is better to first make progress on the understanding side. First, get CoT for understanding working. Then we may be able to extend the method slightly and apply it to generation. So at the end of last year, I started another project: visual understanding. By visual understanding, I more specifically mean vision-language work whose core is truly doing CoT in visual space. The chains of thought in current O-style approaches are basically text. Even if you include images in the input prompt, you can use exactly the same methods as text models to elicit O1-like long CoT.

items.question: How do you think long chains of thought should work for visual understanding?
items.object: Long chains of thought in visual space
items.answer:
All that reasoning is still in text. For many problems that must be solved in image space, the most typical examples are counting, maze solving, connecting lines, recognizing charts, and reading charts. These are very easy for humans. Humans can make circles, marks, and annotations on images; even without marking, merely shifting gaze and attention—count the left side first, then the top, then the right—lets us count or locate things. If I show you a table and ask in which row and column a certain letter is located, or give you a coordinate graph or a clock, humans find those tasks easy. The main reason is that although these problems are simple, they are not simple enough to answer in one shot; you still need reasoning. And that reasoning is not in language space: you must do something in visual space.

So at the end of last year I set up this project to study how to do slow thinking, or long CoT, in visual space. It was inspired by language models: if an action space is missing—such as reflection—add it back. In vision, counting is hard, but recall how people count: circle or mark one item, then mark another, and the problem is solved. How do people solve mazes? Draw a line from the entrance; if you reach a dead end, go back, erase those lines, return to another point, and look again. That gives you an action space. Then I could put those actions into the model through training, using a simple rule-based RL approach: encourage actions that lead to correct answers and suppress those that do not. I even allow it to regret its choices: it can delete marks it has made. Then it has reflection too.

items.question: What do you find most compelling about the generalization of O-like reasoning models?
items.object: Pattern generalization in O-like reasoning models
items.answer:
Compared with solving math or coding problems, I find O's more compelling feature to be its unparalleled generalizability. For example, I trained an O-like model deliberately only on pure mathematics. Then I gave it classical poetry problems, particularly ones with strict prosodic and rhyming requirements—something completely absent from the training data. It elicited a thinking pattern very similar to math solving. It would first draft something, check one requirement at a time, replace parts that failed, then find that the sentence no longer worked, reject both lines entirely, and try again. If that failed, it would reject the whole poem and start over. During the process, it repeatedly checked the word count and whether it met the prompt's requirements. It was almost exactly the same pattern it used in mathematics.

Reflection is only one of many patterns it elicits, though it is the most important. Others include trying another method to verify, a “big loop” that discards everything done before and starts over, and rereading the question repeatedly to see whether it meets the requirements. The same process transfers perfectly to literary tasks even though it was never trained on such poetry. Its generalization is not merely domain generalization—transferring from one kind of math problem to another. That exists, but is not the most compelling part. The more compelling part is pattern generalization. A mode of thinking, such as verification or returning to the previous step, can appear in other problems that may never have occurred in training but are also suitable for that pattern. That is the source of its strong generalization.

I also found a domain where pure-math training cannot generalize: games. Take a model trained only on math, and ask it about a late-stage Dou Dizhu position with both players' hands visible. One side may have two aces and two jacks, and the other has another hand. Ask how the second player should play to win. This paradigm completely fails to grasp the essentials. It does a lot of ineffective thinking and makes basic errors, such as miscounting the cards. Even after one player has gone out, it says that because the two aces have been played, that player cannot stop subsequent plays—although the opponent has already gone out. Its thinking completely misses the point.

Our analysis is that game problems use a different thought paradigm from most math problems: minimax. You must minimize the payoff of the opponent's best solution, so it is a max-min problem. It has not learned that pattern. But if you synthesize many such problems and let it learn them, that kind of thinking is also easy to elicit. It is not that it cannot do it; it needs a class of problems during training that elicits that reasoning paradigm. In other words, its generality is extremely strong—it can generalize across a large area at once.

items.question: How do you interpret your visual-space reasoning project's failure to achieve the broad generalization you see in language models?
items.object: The generalization gap between visual-space reasoning and language-model chain of thought
items.answer:
It sounded beautiful. We could do genuinely visual-space reasoning, without relying on text, and make circles, marks, and annotations directly on the image. But after half a year, let me reveal the actual result: it was not completely ineffective. Training this way really can solve this class of problems. The problem is that whatever kind of data I create, it can solve only that kind of data. It has nothing like the powerful generality we see in language models.

Marking and annotating on images seems usable for many visual-reasoning tasks, so why did synthesizing this data and applying these methods not produce equally strong generalization? Returning to language: our team is broadly fluent in language, vision, and speech, which is a major advantage because we can use cross-modal thinking to diagnose problems. We found that the reflection patterns elicited by O1—patterns empirically shown to work—include many filler phrases like “with” and “alternatively,” and contextual phrases such as “recheck” and “validation.” Although we synthetically create this data in the CoT setup, that is, so to speak, following prior hints: it tells us we can do it this way, but why can it work?

We later found that these patterns already exist, though sparsely, in pretraining corpora. A typical example is highly upvoted contributors on forums like Stack Overflow. They often use similar reasoning processes to answer a problem step by step. Chinese and foreign forums differ greatly here. Chinese forums especially like to say “notice that,” strip away all scaffolding, and make themselves look brilliant: one magical construction solves the problem. If a model sees too much of this sort of text, it is a disaster, because it hides the real thinking process and makes the reasoning extremely jumpy, which is very unfavorable for model learning.

On MathOverflow, by contrast, some high-level contributors begin trying to solve a problem, realize something is wrong, and write, “Wait, I have neglected a factor.” They add that factor, discover their prior method is broken, try this and that, and ultimately present the result in a completely different form, with rechecking as well. Their construction process is in fact exactly like the patterns I constructed. Or perhaps OpenAI also saw much such data in pretraining and therefore designed these patterns: its CoT patterns were not created from nothing; they already existed in pretraining.

We later found this point very important for model generalization. These patterns are rare in pretraining, but produced by different people and institutions and spanning different fields. Although their absolute count is small, in the knowledge and capability system they interlock with other data. So when you elicit them during the CoT stage and then reinforce them through RL, their sparse but widespread presence in pretraining also activates the broad domains connected to them. They become integrated. That, I think, is the primary reason for their strong generalization.

items.question: How do you understand the strengths and limits of O's ability to generalize reasoning patterns?
items.object: Pattern generalization and its limits in O's reasoning
items.answer:
What I find so remarkable about O's generalization is that it seems not merely to generalize by domain. It does generalize from some math problems to other math problems, but that is not its most attractive feature. Its more attractive feature is pattern generalization. A thinking mode—such as checking a calculation or returning to the previous step—can manifest in other problems that may never have appeared in training but are also suited to being solved with that pattern. That is the source of its powerful generalization.

And I also found an area where pure-math data cannot generalize: games. For example, on a model trained purely on math, I deliberately ask about a late-game position in Dou Dizhu, with both sides' cards face up. One side may have two aces and two jacks, while the other has another hand. I ask: if the second player leads, how should they play to win? I found that this paradigm completely fails to grasp the essentials. It does much ineffective thinking and makes many elementary mistakes—such as miscounting cards. Even after one side has played all its cards, it says that because its two aces have already been played, it cannot stop my subsequent plays, when in fact the opponent has already gone out. It produces many such elementary errors, and its thinking entirely misses the point.

Our analysis is that game problems use a thinking paradigm different from most math problems: minimax. It must minimize the payoff of the opponent's optimal solution, so it is a max-min problem. It has not learned this pattern. Of course, if you synthesize a lot of this type of problem and teach it, that type of reasoning is easy to elicit too. It is not that it cannot do it; during training you need this class of problems to elicit its corresponding reasoning paradigm. So its generality is indeed extremely powerful: it can generalize across a large block at once.

items.question: Why do you think reasoning patterns elicited through chain-of-thought training and reinforcement learning can generalize so broadly?
items.object: Pretraining data as the foundation of chain-of-thought generalization
items.answer:
We later found that among the reflection patterns elicited by O1, the ones repeatedly shown to work typically include many words like “with” and “alternatively,” along with contextual phrases such as “recheck” and “validation.” Although we also artificially synthesize such data in the CoT setup, that is, so to speak, following what came before: it tells us this can be done, but why can it work? We later found that these patterns already exist in pretraining data, though in very small quantities.

A typical example is highly upvoted responders on forums such as Stack Overflow, who often use this kind of thinking process to answer questions step by step. Chinese and overseas forums differ a great deal. Chinese forums especially like to say “notice that,” strip away all the scaffolding, and make themselves look very impressive: one magical construction solves the problem. If the model sees too much of that corpus, it is a disaster. It hides the real reasoning process and makes thought extremely jumpy, which is very unfavorable for learning.

But on MathOverflow, some highly skilled answerers begin solving a problem, then realize something is wrong and write, “Wait, I missed a factor.” They add the factor, find their prior method has completely broken, get stuck and try various approaches, eventually present the result in a wholly different form, and recheck it. I find that this construction process is in fact exactly the same as the pattern I constructed. Or, I think OpenAI may well have designed such patterns because it saw a lot of this type of data in pretraining. In other words, its CoT patterns did not arise from nothing; they were already in pretraining.

Thus, when the CoT stage elicits these patterns and RL reinforces them, their scattered presence throughout pretraining also activates broad domains connected to them, bringing them together. items.question: Why do you think O3’s simple image operations generalize better than your earlier approach of circling and pointing on images?
items.object: O3’s image operations compared with programmatically synthesized circle-and-point annotations for visual reasoning
items.answer:
This makes us reflect on why our earlier approach did not work. Circle-and-point annotation on images was all programmatically synthesized data. Its pattern was too fixed. In the pretraining corpus, there is clearly no finely detailed image annotation of this kind—someone genuinely solving a maze from the first step, taking one step in the first image and another in the second. Perhaps animation or video has that form, but it absolutely does not exist in the interleaved image-text data we used often. So what we created was in an awkward position: it represented only itself; it could not activate a broad and widespread class of patterns in the pretraining data. That is why it did not work well.

Now look at the latest O3. It too supports images within long chains of thought, but its way of incorporating images seems more primitive: it only performs very simple operations on the original image, such as cropping and resizing. Yet when we tried it on many problems, it had very strong generalization. Of course, on some problems—for example mazes—it certainly cannot solve them if you do not let it write code. Its upper bound may not be high because it can take only limited actions. But for problems it can solve, its success rate is much higher than that of the system we built at the time.

That is easy to explain from the framework we just discussed. In pretraining corpora, especially interleaved image-text corpora, there are huge amounts of material with one large image followed by enlarged local regions and various explanations underneath. An answerer enlarges different areas: “Look here, this capacitor is burned out”; then another place: “This component has another fault.” There is a huge amount of this kind of corpus. Thus the primitive-looking edits to the original image—only zoom, resize, and crop—strictly follow patterns that exist in natural pretraining data, and so they work better. items.question: Why do you think jointly training diffusion-based image generation with text can damage a model’s language semantics?
items.object: Diffusion-based image generation as a training signal for language models
items.answer: I think the control signal for generating an image itself contains very rich semantics. When you know that, at an appropriate point, you need to generate a particular image, you must fully understand the preceding text, perhaps even an image farther back in the context. You need a complete multimodal understanding to generate that image controllably. But unfortunately, existing methods for generating the image are not able—mainly because of complexity—to provide sufficient computation and information to generate it completely. As a result, the guidance produced by image generation itself is extremely noisy and carries little information. Take diffusion. If you train it jointly with text, diffusion can perform only one denoising step at a time; you sample some T. For most T values, the diffusion process is non-semantic, because the semantics have already been generated and it is merely filling in details. The loss from detail filling, backpropagated into the language component, does not improve language semantics much and may instead damage them.

items.question: Why do you think autoregressive image generation fails to fundamentally solve the problem of harmful supervision in interleaved image-text training?
items.object: Autoregressive image generation and the complexity problem in interleaved image-text training
items.answer: I think autoregression might be somewhat better, but it is not fundamentally better. It is somewhat better because during training its behavior roughly matches inference: it is not producing only the result of one denoising step; it generates patches. Its guidance is therefore relatively clearer and more semantic. But not much better. As I said earlier, images are too complex. Autoregression is still a no-regrets-move mode, so it is unlikely to have very clear behavior. It is like pouring exam questions—math questions, civil-service-exam questions, and so forth—into pretraining but providing no process, only an answer. When the model encounters such a question, it is very confused. You tell it to choose C, but it cannot think of why to choose C within one token. If you add too much of this corpus, two extremes emerge. A stronger model forcibly memorizes the association: next time it sees the question, regardless of anything else, it chooses C. That is overfitting. A weaker model thinks, “C seems different from the others; its answer is longer. Maybe I choose C because it is longer.” It learns false associations. With early small models, when they saw too much one-shot-answer data, they learned strange bugs: for difficult questions, they would always choose the longest option. If it is clear that this form of language training is harmful, it follows that interleaved image-text training is also harmful if you do not solve the CoT or complexity problem. Even with autoregression, even if your supervision signal can generate an image, it cannot actually cover the task in a single step, so many of its outputs are disordered. At best there is no effect. Slightly worse, and it can become very bad.

items.question: Why do you see instructional video as a promising route for expanding visual reasoning?
items.object: Instructional video as a route for expanding visual reasoning
items.answer: The story I was just telling was stuck on one very important point. I presented a seemingly beautiful pattern, but constrained by the limitations of pretraining, it lacked that chain of thought. So its generalization was very limited. And editing the original image—whether circling, annotating, enlarging, or anything else—has too limited an action space. For many problems, I want to make a new draft; I want to regenerate. This led naturally to the idea that the path ahead must split into two routes. First, I need to expand the pretraining corpus, allowing more forms of representation and expanding the action space permitted by the chain of thought. The first route is obvious: video. We know there are large amounts of instructional video with rich, step-by-step thinking processes. In lectures, teachers often use a laser pointer to indicate points, sketch on the screen, draw auxiliary lines, and so on. There is a very rich process. If we introduce that process into training, it must be very helpful. This is a relatively certain route for expanding visual reasoning. Its principal difficulty is cleaning video data.

items.question: How do you think controllable image generation can break the circular dependence between visual generation and visual reasoning?
items.object: Controllable image generation as a way to unlock visual reasoning
items.answer:
The most appealing thing would be highly controllable, free-form generation. Once I can generate freely, my chain of thought is no longer restricted to the original image. I can make concrete, in images, anything I imagine or describe in words, and then reason over it. Visual reasoning could then reach another level. But I wanted to do visual reasoning because visual generation needs a chain of thought, and that problem has not been solved. Yet now visual reasoning also needs generation as an aid. Isn't that circular? So, generally, to unlock thinking, you need one side to be able to get there first.

This year I saw a very good trend. Gemini's highly controllable generation is already quite good. More astonishing is Sora—the latest version. Its image generation and controllability, I think, are already very good, and it seems to be very well integrated with its base model. I am not very clear on how it does this, but since the result is there, I did some related research. Later I found that, if you only care about the quality of controllable generation, it is not such an unsolvable problem. You do not necessarily need to solve CoT, or even Long CoT. You only need to limit the domain of the problem to a range that can be solved in one shot. If you can clean the data well and strictly control its difficulty, highly controllable generation can be achieved over a very large domain.

For example, in a geometric diagram, if I ask you to connect A and B, that requires no thinking. Its complexity is very low. Or take an editing instruction such as removing a person. Of course it depends on the complexity of the background, but in most cases this is also a pure perception-plus-generation task. The problems behind it do not require much reasoning.

Previously, we did not particularly emphasize controlling the purity and difficulty of this data well. We more often mixed together all kinds of internet corpora, with images and text interleaved in a mess. Many news articles use images unrelated to the text, or some images are memes. Much of that corpus is very difficult; it is not something a single-step generation can accomplish. We mixed all of this together, so the model struggled greatly, and its controllability became very poor. This also shows that overseas companies are ahead of us in a lot of technology or understanding. Since they have made it work, after seeing their results I can roughly infer that this approach still has a chance based on current architectures. The core is still to get the data right.

items.question: What do you value most in an image-generation model intended to support reasoning?
items.object: Semantic instruction following versus aesthetics in image generation for reasoning
items.answer:
This year we released an editing model. The data is still very rough and dirty, but its results are already beyond what the generation-understanding integrated models I worked on at the time could do. Of course, this is not yet fully generation-understanding integrated; it is still somewhat assembled like building blocks. But we will soon also release a model built on this model that can synthesize a large amount of data, use those correlations, and train an integrated model on that data. At least for some simple tasks, it can do very well. That is a very encouraging signal.

Our company does not care that much about aesthetics and such things—we are pursuing AGI. But purely in terms of image structure and faithfulness to instructions, I think it can now be done very well. At least for simple problems—what I call instruction-type problems, problems requiring no reasoning—it can do very well. These are things like constantly moving this over there, or generating something with X on the left, Y in the middle, and Z above. Or, for example, in a bar chart, draw a horizontal line so that the bar on the right points to the coordinate axis on the left. It can handle such instructions very well.

Many people care more about aesthetics, such as whether faces are distorted. But if your goal is reasoning, that is not the key. The key is to complete these instruction-following tasks as they should be completed—at least semantically. Quality is not that important; having a rough sense and direction is enough.

Once you solve this step, the most exciting next question is whether a model like this can enter the reasoning chain of thought. If I have such a model, and can also achieve preliminary generation-understanding—by which I mean without CoT, a generation-and-understanding model that can simply execute instruction-type prompts well—I can use it as a starting point. It can produce outputs wherever desired. Those outputs do not have to be generated correctly in one pass, because the later chain of thought can revise them. Then you realize it can do understanding in a broader sense. For example, for problems requiring spatial imagination or drawing a sketch before they can be carried out or solved, with this capability, I am not saying it will solve them especially well, but at least they become solvable.

items.question: How do you assess Transformer long context as a model of human memory?
items.object: Long context in Transformers compared with human memory
items.answer: When people ask why long context is important, most companies or institutions, as I understand it, mean it is important for applications. We have massive reference information for many applications, while the model itself does not know domain-specific information about your particular environment or use case. Another major issue today is hallucination, so people like to throw in as much reference material as possible. Under current architectures, the main way to accommodate that material is to put it into the context. But honestly, I have a different view from the perspective of the development of intelligence. Transformers have serious problems modeling long context. For a standard Transformer, context size grows proportionally with the data; it performs no compression and does not prune information. Humans are very different. After a meeting, most people record the most important or memorable details. When you watch a movie, you see all the details, but you certainly do not firmly remember how many water glasses were on the table at a particular minute. Human memory is hierarchical. Short-term memory—working memory—is generally thought to last only two to four seconds. When copying down a phone number, it can preserve it losslessly or precisely. But once you have copied the number, if it is not important, you will not remember it. What is really powerful is humans' intermediate-term memory, which may range from seconds to weeks. Its key characteristics are continuity, forgetting, and a very strong ability to grasp the important points. People remember information that is most likely to be useful in the future, and repeated stimulation strengthens such memory. The typical example is coding: people do not need to remember an entire repository and everything in it. They only need a general grasp and can begin working. When they wake up and return to work the next day, they can seamlessly continue the previous day's work. They do not need to reread all the code for every task, as our current base models do. But if they go on vacation for a few weeks, they may forget everything and have to review it all again. Finally, people have long-term memory: some things, through repeated stimulation and deep impressions, become memories that last a lifetime. In neural-network terms, perhaps they become solidified in the parameters. By contrast, traditional Transformer architectures seem, by this analogy, to have only short-term memory—but short-term memory that is far too long. I once estimated that, at a certain bitrate, visual signals alone over two to four seconds might occupy roughly 300,000 tokens. Yet today, long context means 100,000, millions, or even tens of millions of tokens. Making context longer often only solves the problem of fitting the information in; it does not solve what you can get from that information. We seem able to do only the simplest retrieval. Slightly more complex reasoning problems cannot be handled; it does not solve how to use the information well.
