items.question: Why do you regard the insistence on lossless retention in Transformer context as an obstacle to intelligence?
items.object: Context interference, compression, and retrieval-oriented training
items.answer: In current mainstream architectures, especially relatively small models, performance declines as context grows. One major reason is context interference. If you have a model answer a math exam one question at a time, clearing the context after each question, you get one level of performance. If it answers continuously from the first question to the last, its early performance may be similar, but if there are 100 or 200 questions, performance drops sharply later on. Analysis of attention shows obvious distractibility: with too many similar contexts left uncleared, when looking at later questions it constantly attends to earlier ones, and expends much effort avoiding interference. This makes efficiency drop sharply as context lengthens. And that is before the familiar quadratic-complexity problem of attention. Complexity is not my main concern; I care more about the modeling problem of intelligence itself. This alone shows the approach is wrong. We often say compression is what wins. If information is not processed and compressed—losslessly or lossily, the principle is the same—if you do not derive a more concise representation of it, intelligence cannot emerge. But when you model context with a Transformer, its memory capacity grows in lockstep with information, so it has neither pressure nor a loss that drives compression. Especially if your tasks include many retrieval tasks, the model learns an even stronger bias: it cannot forget anything, because training constantly tests retrieval, such as needle-in-a-haystack problems. But this is not intelligence; it is a regression of intelligence. This insistence on not forgetting, or on only losslessness, obstructs progress.

items.question: How would you design a long-context system that can forget details while still retrieving what it needs?
items.object: A long-context architecture using specialized language models and selective retrieval
items.answer: Many people recognize this and try to use RNNs—humans can be regarded as an RNN with an infinite sequence—to replace some Transformers. The most classic examples are variants of linear functions; a linear function can be viewed as an RNN. They have achieved some effects in practice, though as far as I know they are still used relatively little. My view is that these architectures are all good. But the core difficulty or key point of modeling long context is fundamentally not there, and even many benchmarks this year have misconceptions. For example, many people mix RNN-like methods, such as linear Transformers, with ordinary Transformers, because otherwise retrieval tasks cannot be done and needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks are hard to pass. But is that benchmark really important? In today's era of function calling, long context can fully use multiple models; the retrieval task can be solved through multi-model collaboration. Imagine giving someone a book. After reading it, if they have to write a summary but need to quote some excellent sentences, they have forgotten many details, perhaps even the wording. They do not directly recite the sentence from memory—that easily hallucinates, because human memory is limited and people forget. They flip through the book chapter by chapter, following their impression of where a good plot point was, and copy good content from it. You can understand flipping through a book as a function call or RAG. But in my view it may be more complex: it involves shifting attention from global attention to a local region, with the global attention directing that local focus. I could model it as two LMs. Each LM uses only a relatively short-context ordinary Transformer plus an infinite-context linear Transformer. I would not, as in popular architectures like Gemini, directly use a full-size Transformer plus a full-size linear Transformer. That would merely be a trick; your memory size would still become very large, retaining all the drawbacks I just described. So I deliberately use a very small-context ordinary Transformer to model short-term memory, and an infinite-sequence model such as a linear Transformer to model global information. I first go through the book and get an overall impression. If I want to open a certain page, I trigger an action and find it: perhaps something around 20% of the book is important to me. For another LM, I can try the same architecture; it looks only at that 20%. I see whether it has what I want. If it does, it directly feeds back to my main Transformer—the lower, infinite-sequence one. If not, the lower one says it found nothing good, and I look somewhere else, because I retain a general impression of where something good may be. In this way, I cleverly solve it by extending the chain of thought. At no point do I store the entire book intact. On the contrary, I extend the chain of thought, and that chain has tools—not only tools like RAG, but also calling another LM. This is also why I think the human brain has relatively fine-grained specialization across regions, rather than one brain region handling every modality and task: it may be a more context-efficient approach.

items.question: How would you use separate planning and execution models to make a reasoning model work beyond its context limit?
items.object: A two-model planning-and-execution architecture for long reasoning
items.answer: Suppose I tell you that I have a reasoning base model with only, say, 180K or 182K context. How can I make it reason for that long? There is a very simple approach: use two models. One model does planning, and the other does the concrete solving. Each time the planning model searches a branch, after entering that branch, the subsequent concrete calculation is performed by the second model. That model has only limited context, context generated from a summary by the planning model. It computes a result—perhaps it finds the answer, or perhaps not, but feeds back some ideas—and reports that result to the main, controlling model. That model then plans a second path based on the feedback and sends it to the execution model. This path is unrelated to the preceding path. Thus the second model, which performs calculation and derivation, need not retain the context of the previous step. It only needs the necessary information sent by the controlling agent. This is like humans: when doing the second problem, why dwell on the first? If you explored one path for the first problem and it was a dead end, why keep dwelling on it when you calculate again? The second model is like human attention shifting contexts. Humans have strong situation isolation. While I am talking to you now, there may have been many issues in my office just now, but at this moment I am not thinking about them; they are not in my context. In this way, if your search unfolds like a binary tree, originally you would need to flatten every path in the entire tree, and your CoT might need tens of millions of tokens. Now you need only logarithmic scale: from the top node to the bottom node, only log scale. The planning model needs only high-level structure—what paths were searched and what results were obtained—while the execution-and-derivation model needs only the part it currently cares about. Its historical calculations need not be stored at all. This greatly reduces chain-of-thought length. But the most important point is that many people dismiss this architecture, saying, 'Isn't this just a pieced-together agent?'

items.question: Why do you see a two-model reasoning system with limited contexts as an end-to-end approach?

items.answer: I limit the context length of these two models: neither can ever exceed that length. But they can communicate with each other and repeatedly clear their contexts. items.question: How do you understand the importance of architectural innovations such as linear attention in relation to algorithms and systems?
items.object: The relationship between neural network architecture, algorithms, and systems
items.answer: I keep emphasizing one idea: architecture is not important; architecture serves algorithms and systems. Whatever algorithm you have, you can do what that algorithm enables. This includes linear Transformers. Why do I think they are not fundamental at all? Because today's algorithm is autoregressive NTP. If you do not use that algorithm—say Hinton's feed-forward-only set of methods, the no-backpropagation algorithm; I have forgotten the name a bit, I think it is called FFA—then you do not need linear attention at all. Any ordinary RNN works, because it does not backpropagate through history. If that algorithm ultimately works, online learning can be done directly too. There would be no separate training and inference phases; training is also a kind of inference. So architecture serves the algorithm. Because you have next prediction and need parallelization, you must impose certain requirements on the RNN structure: it must take a separable form, which is why linear attention emerged.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between advances in modalities and advances in training methods in the evolution of large models?
items.object: The evolution of large models through modality and optimization methods
items.answer: Looking at the evolution of large models today, I see two core axes: optimization methods and modality. The representative event from zero to one on the optimization axis was the discovery of next-token prediction. The starting point on the modality axis was natural language. Development has been a kind of spiral ascent along both. Because next-token prediction works very well on text, more and more people have researched how to transfer similar paradigms to more modalities. In that transfer they repeatedly hit walls; after enough failures, people question whether the paradigm and training work at all. Another group focuses mainly on language itself and studies language reasoning, especially math, and also finds problems with next-token prediction. So the shared conclusion is that compression-based training is not enough; we need RL. RL directly optimizes toward objectives instead of using an indirect optimization method. Objective-oriented optimization suddenly activated many ideas. Language-model reasoning improved greatly, and many formerly intractable multimodal generation-understanding integration problems suddenly began to make sense because reasoning models existed. Today we are still exploring the limits of RL as a training algorithm, but more and more people are finding that this algorithm is not perfect either.

items.question: Why do you see autonomous learning as a necessary direction beyond current rule-based reinforcement learning?
items.object: Rule-based reinforcement learning and the need for autonomous learning

For me, the least sensible part of current language work is that only rule-based approaches, and some approaches such as inverse reinforcement learning, work. This differs greatly from human learning and is very limited. Most notably, rule-based methods cannot handle things without evaluation criteria or clear evaluation criteria. You can model these with models, but their behavior is easily hacked. For humans, understanding self-worth and judging correctness more often relies on the brain itself. As the joke goes, people do not do everything to serve KPIs. There must be self-awareness and an internal drive. In other words, this evaluation module very likely should not be external. Our current rule-based methods are all external; reward models are also external—distilling external preferences and then supervising itself. We lack a truly endogenous drive.

Many people may say this is unimportant and current methods are sufficient. But in engineering practice, if you keep following rule-based methods, you run into a scaling problem again: not model scaling or data scaling, but environment scaling. To solve programming problems, you have to build environments. For one project, you need to set up the whole Docker input/output and test-data stack, and then you produce one data point. That is far too inefficient. As far as I know, many large companies now do this, hiring many engineers to write projects one by one. Companies focused on programming may be good at it, but it is ultimately unlike humans. Humans do not learn through countless externally hand-built environments; they are self-driven. They read articles, build environments themselves, learn from environmental feedback, and that learning is definitely not merely binary.

The biggest problem facing the previous or current generation of rule-based RL is still that environments cannot be scaled up; you need many people to annotate. Real humans should be able to explore autonomously in a space and continuously improve through communicating with the environment. There are two technical details involved. One is modeling infinitely long context: the real environment is an infinitely long, dynamic sequence, not an interface in steady state. The second is learning algorithms, especially how to improve from natural-language or unstructured feedback, and how to design intrinsic rewards. Intrinsic rewards are what drive a model to update its own weights and parameters to adapt to the world. These are the problems the next generation of autonomous learning must solve. We often bind autonomous learning and online learning together because, if you solve autonomy, why not put it into the real environment and let it play? Then it becomes an online mode. This is our next step and a direction in which I will invest heavily.

items.question: Why do you consider learning from natural-language feedback a foundational problem for autonomous models?
items.object: Natural-language feedback and scalar rewards in reinforcement learning
items.answer:
Even one very small issue in this large loop is hard today: how to obtain feedback from human natural language. Suppose I write an essay. My teacher says the first paragraph is good; the second uses rhetoric a little excessively; the third does not connect well with the context; the fourth has typos; and overall it feels somewhat dry and too short. The teacher evaluates my essay across many different dimensions. But RL today separately weights each comment: this is worth 0.1 points, that adds 0.5, and in the end it says the answer scored three points. It completely loses the rich dimensions of the evaluation.

This is the dilemma of general-purpose reward models today: you can indeed evaluate an answer on many dimensions, but there is no good way to use those dimensions. In the end they are all weighted into a dry number. The model does not know how that number was calculated; it can only guess through many samples. It inefficiently has to infer your scoring rules and each scoring factor—whether you scored its first paragraph, second paragraph, overall style, or narrative logic. All this information is lost. It cannot obtain feedback from that single number. Even this step does not yet have a relatively perfect solution. There are many papers on it, but none widely recognized in industry as doing it well.

Natural-language feedback is especially a key area of my current research. To truly realize autonomous learning, the prerequisite technologies are still extensive. One of the most important is communicating with the environment, much of which is natural language. You need the ability to obtain feedback from natural language: if a leader criticizes your work as wrong, you need to know in which direction to improve. That is foundational. Of course, this is only a small technical detail among many that must be broken through.

items.question: How do you see the possibilities and challenges of an autonomously learning agent tailored to a company?
items.object: Autonomously learning agents customized for a company
items.answer: It could be highly customized. This agent would be an employee of your company—tailored specifically for you. Of course, there would be many systems challenges: how do you copy it or migrate it? God left a big bug in creating humans: one person's memories cannot easily be given to another person. After autonomous learning is achieved, it has similar problems: how do you merge two people, two individuals? That is also difficult, though it depends on how it is modeled.

items.question: Why do you think developing the current generation of AI approaches remains necessary when future advances could be disruptive?
items.object: The value of developing the current generation of AI approaches for future advances
items.answer: That is very hard to predict. With every iteration, the hardest thing is understanding. It could be disruptive or incremental; it might be a small revision, even just a matter of a loss function. Solve one loss function and it is done. It may be simple or very complex. But historically, the crucial point is understanding. Only after you have made the previous generation fairly complete can you fully understand its boundaries and problems. That know-how of understanding is the key. So in any case, you have to do the previous generation. That is why.

items.question: How do you interpret the algorithmic progression implied by OpenAI’s five levels of intelligence?
items.object: The algorithmic progression implied by OpenAI’s five levels of intelligence
items.answer: My understanding is that, if you insist on using OpenAI's five levels, the implication is that every generation of levels requires a completely new algorithm. In the chatbot era, it was essentially next-token prediction. The reason it insists on separating out its o-series as 'reason' is that it tries to center on RL, and RL will scale more and more going forward.

items.object: AI-agent autonomy and the limitations of current reasoning systems
items.answer: I think the definition of agent particularly emphasizes autonomy. I should not need humans to design so many environments or define so many rules. Of course, compared with NTP, NTP requires not only giving it the objective but also making it memorize the path to reach that objective—the exact route.

items.question: How do you distinguish a true agent era from the AI agents being built today?
items.object: The agent era versus today's AI agents
items.answer: I think you have to find your own objectives, explore yourself, and learn your own reward function. That is the agent era: because an agent is defined as being able to work independently, it must be able to self-evolve and therefore needs such a mechanism—a new algorithm. But what we call agents today are more applications. They assemble a complex pipeline, or use the RL mechanisms of today's reason-model generation. People are broadly pushing tools and function calls into lang-T; that means making function calls more intelligent, invoking them when needed. This generation of agents is still more an idea of the reason era: connect a series of systems, give them a unified KPI, let them output however they like, and finish once they maximize that KPI. That is still reason-era thinking.

items.question: How do you distinguish the tool use of reasoning-era agents from the agents people built with LangChain?
items.object: LangChain-era agents and reinforcement-learning-based tool use in reasoning models
items.answer: I think it goes a step further than LangChain. In the LangChain era, some people also called it agent, but it was fully hand-crafted pipelines. Those agents were essentially still chatbots—things from the next-token-prediction era, where people used prompt engineering to glue several flows together. That belonged to that era. In the reason era, we now emphasize models actively calling tools. But it is not merely calling them; the call is not triggered by a prompt. Rather, we expand its action space to include calling, and it autonomously triggers it through RL. It calls when it believes calling will be better, following the principle of maximizing the RL objective. If it finds calling is worse than not calling, it will not call. In effect, the model learns this behavior.

items.question: Do you expect multimodal models, autonomous-driving systems, and robot intelligence ultimately to converge on the same form as AGI?
items.object: The eventual convergence of multimodal models, autonomous driving, robotics, and AGI
items.answer: Yes. In fact, these fields are all making an early start. Our intelligence level is far from the point where we should be discussing this; everyone is still struggling with vision. Machine control started earlier. Its domains are generally either relatively constrained problems or relatively constrained control scenarios. For autonomous driving, the control dimensions are relatively low, and the driving scenarios are relatively constrained compared with general-purpose robotics. So it has an opportunity to get moving earlier, using some rule-based methods and modular decomposition to get a system running first. But look at the current autonomous-driving trend: it too is moving toward end to end. When all these things become fully end to end and you also need to integrate visual reasoning or multimodal reasoning, you find that they have the same form as the AGI end state. Robotics even more so. Right now, because we cannot do it well, you can only make a robot fold a quilt or run—like running a marathon—and add little-cerebellum-type components. That is only because the technology is not there yet, but it does not prevent these things from already having some applications. So they started early, and their routes may not follow the AGI main line I just described, but ultimately they will merge at some point.
